# The Mid-Rehab Checkpoint: ~85% MV Around Day 10-14 for Hamstring-Type Injuries

**What it is** — Harries gives a calendar anchor, matched to force-production, reactive-strength and healing-time criteria. Inference: these line up with the general 75-85% MV gate (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]). Inference: his "this type of injury" reads as the hamstring-type strains of Cases 1-2. Describing session 5 (stated as "identical to session five in case one," ~19:47-19:56), he says it "probably represents a typical mid stage max velocity progression for this type of injury at about the 10 [to] 14 day post injury mark" (~19:56-20:04) and, discussing the same session a few lines later, that it "typifies the point in rehab where you push towards around about 85% max velocity at that day 14 type mark, plus or minus, but rarely would you go beyond that. Most would consider this a bit of a sound ceiling until further force production or reactive strength criteria are confirmed, as well as some adequate time for biological healing" (~20:40-21:02). He calls the timing "typical" (19:58); "most would consider" refers to the ~85% ceiling (20:53). He adds that the session structure "could be employed slightly earlier or held slightly later, depending on how the athlete's responding" (~20:08-20:14). The transcript literally reads "10 day 14 post injury mark," almost certainly an ASR-dropped "to"; read as "10 to 14 day."

**Why it works** — Practitioner ceiling. The day-10-14 anchor itself is stated as "typical", with no stated dispute. He frames ~85% as a ceiling to hold until force-production and reactive-strength criteria are confirmed and healing time has passed (20:51-21:00). He gives no physiological mechanism for why day 10-14 specifically is the natural point for this pause; the timing is presented as his stated clinical experience ("most would consider," "typical"), not a derived rule.

**When to apply** — As a rough calendar anchor for planning when a hamstring-type strain rehab should reach the 75-85% MV gate, so force-production and reactive-strength testing (Nordic, isometric benchmarks, hop test; see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]) can be scheduled around day 10-14 rather than left open-ended. Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that Baylor has no documented phased RTP timeline of its own yet; this gives a starting calendar reference to validate against Baylor's own returning-athlete data.

**When NOT to apply** — This is stated for "this type of injury," meaning the hamstring-type strains of Cases 1-2. Harries treats the calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]], discussed later in the same module, ~27:00 onward) as a deliberately different, lower-frequency injury pattern; do not apply the day-10-14 anchor to that case, or to a joint/ligament case such as [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]], which was still brace-restricted and straight-line-only through session 6. This is expert opinion ("most would consider"), not a validated cutoff. The 20:40-21:02 passage itself names no specific numbers; it defers to the force-production and reactive-strength criteria set out in [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]], whose specific benchmark figures (1.7-1.8x BW calf, 80-85% pre-injury hamstring) that entry already flags as AFL-context, citation-free numbers. Confidence is capped `contested` here for the same reason (see that entry's Related link to Wollin 2020 for a closer evidence base on hamstring strength benchmarking).

**Example** — In [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] and [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]], session 5 (identical structure in both) sits at this checkpoint: six 60 m strides, two each at 70-75%, 75-80% and ~82.5% MV.

**Related** — [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] (the general force-production/healing/reactive-strength criteria this checkpoint time-anchors); [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] (the calf case this checkpoint explicitly does not describe); [[research-papers/wollin-2020-a-novel-hamstring-strain-injury-prevention-system-post-match-strength-testing-for-secondar]]

# The Five-Element Case-Review Structure

**What it is** — Harries reviews each of his four case studies through the same five elements, stated explicitly: "the rehab timeline, which is a high-level overview of the return to play calendar"; "the loading structure. So how was loading planned and how was it progressed across on-field rehab"; "the progression of maximum velocity and how those linear running intensities were increased"; "our multi-directional speed and agility progressions and how we developed acceleration, deceleration and change of direction"; and "for each case study... the sport-specific skill progressions and how the technical and tactical tasks were integrated" (~00:39-01:17). He also states the cases were deliberately chosen to minimize individual complexity so the framework's application would read clearly, while acknowledging "no case is ever entirely free from complexity" (~01:21-01:45), and that he included cases that "didn't go perfect to show that the real world is not always that way" (~01:45-01:51).

**Why it works** — No stated mechanism; this is a presentation and documentation structure Harries uses for teaching, not a claim about rehab physiology or efficacy.

**When to apply** — As a template for a Baylor RTP case log or after-action review: for a returning athlete, record (1) the RTP timeline/calendar, (2) the loading structure and how it was progressed, (3) max-velocity progression, (4) MDSA progression, and (5) sport-skill progression. Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates "do not yet exist" at Applied Performance and are named as unfinished Phase 2 work; this five-element structure is a ready-made scaffold specifically for RTP case documentation, distinct from that broader reporting gap.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a presentation structure built for four selected, deliberately simplified cases, not a validated clinical documentation standard, and Harries does not claim it captures everything relevant to an actual RTP decision. It has no explicit slot for the competitive-exposure/hesitation criteria in [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]] and [[heuristic--hesitation-signals-unready-but-is-unmeasured]] (those show up folded into the sport-skill-progression element in practice, not as their own listed element). Do not treat the five elements as exhaustive without adding Baylor's own required documentation fields (medical clearance sign-off, testing-battery results, incident/mechanism detail) alongside them.

**Example** — Each of the four case-study entries in this folder roughly follows this order in its own body sections (rehab timeline folded into "What it is," then MV progression, MDSA, sport-specific skill as separate paragraphs), though none names the structure explicitly and none gives "loading structure" its own separate paragraph the way Harries' five-element list implies; see [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] for the closest match.

**Related** — [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]; [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]]; [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]; [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] (reciprocal link suggestion: each could add "documented using [[framework--five-element-case-review-structure]]" to its own Related line)

input.old_string:
**When to apply** — Use from ~70-75% MV (Level 3) onward, once an athlete moves "beyond around about this 70 to 75% of max velocity" (~17:01-17:07), as the standard method for prescribing and verifying max-velocity exposures. At later levels, continue shortening the acceleration-phase distance (while keeping the target maintenance speed) to increase acceleration magnitude, and build in fatiguing conditions before high-%MV maintenance-phase reps.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries explicitly becomes "far less rigid" with these time targets in later rehab stages. He does not replace the target time with a bandwidth; he adds a percentage bandwidth in addition to the target completion time, "albeit with a ceiling on what is an acceptable progression for that session" (~20:30-20:48), because forcing a fixed time can push an athlete faster than they are comfortable with or unnecessarily hold them back; he pairs each rep with a conversation (how did that feel, are you comfortable) rather than treating the stopwatch number as absolute (~20:17-20:48). Do not apply this as a rigid pass/fail number in late-stage rehab without that check-in, and do not drop the target time itself once the bandwidth is added.

# Broken-Stride Timing: Time Only the Middle Phase

**What it is** — Once an athlete progresses beyond ~70-75% of MV, Harries moves from full-distance timed repeats to a "broken stride": a run divided into an acceleration phase, a speed-maintenance phase and a deceleration phase, e.g. 60 m split into 20 m / 20 m / 20 m (adjustable, e.g. 15/10/15 to demand a more aggressive acceleration into the same target speed) (~17:01-18:20). Critically, he times only the middle (speed-maintenance) phase, not the whole distance, because that isolates the actual target speed from the acceleration and deceleration mechanics around it. Worked example: hitting 2.88-3.0 seconds across the middle phase equates to ~24-25 km/h, which is ~70-75% of that athlete's MV (~18:29-18:51); the next progression steps require 2.77-2.88 seconds through the same phase, pushing speed up roughly 1 km/h more. He prefers a stopwatch for immediate feedback, using GPS/video as a secondary confirmation of peak velocity, not the primary control method (~18:51-19:17).

**Why it works** — Inference (entry writer's rationale, not stated by Harries this way): timing the whole distance conflates three different physical demands (accelerating, holding speed, decelerating) into one number, so it can't precisely control what speed was actually reached in the middle. Harries' own stated reason is narrower: the middle-phase time is set "to equate to a given speed through that middle distance... that's going to correspond to the athlete's max velocity" (~18:18-18:29) - i.e. it gives a direct, controllable readout of the target velocity.

**When to apply** — Use from ~70-75% MV (Level 3) onward, once an athlete moves "beyond around about this 70 to 75% of max velocity" (~17:01-17:07), as the standard method for prescribing and verifying max-velocity exposures. At later levels, continue shortening the acceleration-phase distance (while keeping the target maintenance speed) to increase acceleration magnitude, and build in fatiguing conditions before high-%MV maintenance-phase reps.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries explicitly becomes "far less rigid" with these time targets in later rehab stages. He does not replace the target time with a bandwidth; he adds a percentage bandwidth in addition to the target completion time, "albeit with a ceiling on what is an acceptable progression for that session" (~20:30-20:48), because forcing a fixed time can push an athlete faster than they are comfortable with or unnecessarily hold them back; he pairs each rep with a conversation (how did that feel, are you comfortable) rather than treating the stopwatch number as absolute (~20:17-20:48). Do not apply this as a rigid pass/fail number in late-stage rehab without that check-in, and do not drop the target time itself once the bandwidth is added.

**Example** — See [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] for the objective criteria Harries applies before letting an athlete progress past the 70-75% zone this protocol is designed to hit precisely.

14	# The Mid-Rehab Checkpoint: ~85% MV Around Day 10-14 for Hamstring-Type Injuries
15	
16	**What it is** — Harries gives a calendar anchor, matched to force-production, reactive-strength and healing-time criteria. Inference: these line up with the general 75-85% MV gate (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]). Inference: his "this type of injury" reads as the hamstring-type strains of Cases 1-2. Describing session 5 (stated as "identical to session five in case one," ~19:47-19:56), he says it "probably represents a typical mid stage max velocity progression for this type of injury at about the 10 [to] 14 day post injury mark" (~19:56-20:04) and, discussing the same session a few lines later, that it "typifies the point in rehab where you push towards around about 85% max velocity at that day 14 type mark, plus or minus, but rarely would you go beyond that. Most would consider this a bit of a sound ceiling until further force production or reactive strength criteria are confirmed, as well as some adequate time for biological healing" (~20:40-21:02). He calls the timing "typical" (19:58); "most would consider" refers to the ~85% ceiling (20:53). He adds that the session structure "could be employed slightly earlier or held slightly later, depending on how the athlete's responding" (~20:08-20:14). The transcript literally reads "10 day 14 post injury mark," almost certainly an ASR-dropped "to"; read as "10 to 14 day."
17	
18	**Why it works** — Practitioner ceiling. The day-10-14 anchor itself is stated as "typical", with no stated dispute. He frames ~85% as a ceiling to hold until force-production and reactive-strength criteria are confirmed and healing time has passed (20:51-21:00). He gives no physiological mechanism for why day 10-14 specifically is the natural point for this pause; the timing is presented as his stated clinical experience ("most would consider," "typical"), not a derived rule.
19	
20	**When to apply** — As a rough calendar anchor for planning when a hamstring-type strain rehab should reach the 75-85% MV gate, so force-production and reactive-strength testing (Nordic, isometric benchmarks, hop test; see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]) can be scheduled around day 10-14 rather than left open-ended. Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that Baylor has no documented phased RTP timeline of its own yet; this gives a starting calendar reference to validate against Baylor's own returning-athlete data.
21

14	# Broken-Stride Timing: Time Only the Middle Phase
15	
16	**What it is** — Once an athlete progresses beyond ~70-75% of MV, Harries moves from full-distance timed repeats to a "broken stride": a run divided into an acceleration phase, a speed-maintenance phase and a deceleration phase, e.g. 60 m split into 20 m / 20 m / 20 m (adjustable, e.g. 15/10/15 to demand a more aggressive acceleration into the same target speed) (~17:01-18:20). Critically, he times only the middle (speed-maintenance) phase, not the whole distance, because that isolates the actual target speed from the acceleration and deceleration mechanics around it. Worked example: hitting 2.88-3.0 seconds across the middle phase equates to ~24-25 km/h, which is ~70-75% of that athlete's MV (~18:29-18:51); the next progression steps require 2.77-2.88 seconds through the same phase, pushing speed up roughly 1 km/h more. He prefers a stopwatch for immediate feedback, using GPS/video as a secondary confirmation of peak velocity, not the primary control method (~18:51-19:17).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Inference (entry writer's rationale, not stated by Harries this way): timing the whole distance conflates three different physical demands (accelerating, holding speed, decelerating) into one number, so it can't precisely control what speed was actually reached in the middle. Harries' own stated reason is narrower: the middle-phase time is set "to equate to a given speed through that middle distance... that's going to correspond to the athlete's max velocity" (~18:18-18:29) - i.e. it gives a direct, controllable readout of the target velocity.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Use from ~70-75% MV (Level 3) onward, once an athlete moves "beyond around about this 70 to 75% of max velocity" (~17:01-17:07), as the standard method for prescribing and verifying max-velocity exposures. At later levels, continue shortening the acceleration-phase distance (while keeping the target maintenance speed) to increase acceleration magnitude, and build in fatiguing conditions before high-%MV maintenance-phase reps. In the strides, recovery lengthens to a walk-back between reps, with a check-in conversation before speed is raised (Part 3 19:47-20:12).
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Harries explicitly becomes "far less rigid" with these time targets in later rehab stages. He does not replace the target time with a bandwidth; he adds a percentage bandwidth in addition to the target completion time, "albeit with a ceiling on what is an acceptable progression for that session" (~20:30-20:48), because forcing a fixed time can push an athlete faster than they are comfortable with or unnecessarily hold them back; he pairs each rep with a conversation (how did that feel, are you comfortable) rather than treating the stopwatch number as absolute (~19:57-20:12). Do not apply this as a rigid pass/fail number in late-stage rehab without that check-in, and do not drop the target time itself once the bandwidth is added.
23	
24	**Example** — See [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] for the objective criteria Harries applies before letting an athlete progress past the 70-75% zone this protocol is designed to hit precisely.

Case 2, week 3: a small on-field rehab session early in the week, a return to partial training midweek, then "a larger combined rehab session with modified team training" at week's end (~17:45-17:56). Case 2, week 4: two non-consecutive training days then two consecutive days, the second-to-last being "a captain's run walkthrough style session, though very low intensity," followed by return to play in a match (~17:56-18:10). Case 1, week 3: "a high moderate high structure, including partial training exposure in the midweek, and a heavier modified training session on the weekend" (~05:18-05:27). Case 1, week 4: "one light partial session, a full training midweek, and a walkthrough style session... And then they played their game at the end of the week" (~05:27-05:37). Case 4, week 7 (the RTP week): "a small session early in the week, a moderate session mid-week, which was aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season," then return to play at week's end (~38:13-38:26).
17	
18	Case 4 (knee), week 5, is a separate pattern, not an instance of team-rhythm alignment: running frequency was deliberately reduced to two larger-load sessions "in order to make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions," explicitly to bridge into "a larger rehab focus session which was designed as a session that was comparable to match loads in order to prepare for a return to play," planned for week 6 (~37:24-38:11). That week-6 session is a pre-RTP match-load rehearsal, distinct from the team-week-shaping pattern described above.
19	
20	**Why it works** — For the Case 4 frequency cut, Harries states the reason directly: reducing running frequency let him "make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions" so there was "a nice little progression into" the larger, match-comparable session planned for the following week (~37:26-37:55). For the broader practice of shaping rehab-week structure around the team's rhythm, his only stated reason is the week-7 mid-week session "aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season" (~38:20-38:22); he gives no further explicit rationale for the general practice. Inference (entry writer's): tying rehab-session load to the team's own hard/light day pattern lets the returning athlete's tolerance build in step with what full training will actually demand in the week he returns, rather than on a schedule disconnected from it.
21	
22	**When to apply** — When designing a returning athlete's week once he is off an isolated running-only schedule and beginning to overlap with team sessions (typically mid-to-late rehab, alongside modified/partial training participation). Eric's review (Review and Plan line 75, "Linear → undulating" row): "You already undulate load across the team week"; the gap it fills is "the same logic applied to one returning player, anchored to the team's Tue/Wed high, Thu low pattern." That remark is about linear-then-undulating MV progression (see [[heuristic--linear-then-undulating-mv-progression]]), not this week-shaping pattern directly. 23	
24	**When NOT to apply** — Harries never states this as a fixed template; no claim is made that a "high-moderate-high" week or a captain's-run walkthrough is required, and the specific weekly shapes differ across all three cases that show them, tracking each athlete's own timeline and injury type. Case outcomes only (n=3), no outcome data. Do not import a specific case's weekly pattern wholesale as a template; use the underlying idea, build the rehab week around the team's actual week, and rebuild the specific days for each returning athlete.

# Fitting Rehab Sessions Into the Team's Own Training Week

**What it is** — In Cases 1, 2 and 4, once the athlete overlaps with team training, the rehab week is shaped around the team's week: Case 2 "started to fall into the team's training structure a bit more" (17:40-17:44), and Case 4's RTP week was "aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season" (38:20-38:22). Case 2, week 3: a small on-field rehab session early in the week, a return to partial training midweek, then "a larger combined rehab session with modified team training" at week's end (~17:45-17:56). Case 2, week 4: two non-consecutive training days then two consecutive days, the second-to-last being "a captain's run walkthrough style session, though very low intensity," followed by return to play in a match (~17:56-18:10). Case 1, week 3: "a high moderate high structure, including partial training exposure in the midweek, and a heavier modified training session on the weekend" (~05:18-05:27). Case 1, week 4: "one light partial session, a full training midweek, and a walkthrough style session... And then they played their game at the end of the week" (~05:27-05:37). Case 4, week 7 (the RTP week): "a small session early in the week, a moderate session mid-week, which was aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season," then return to play at week's end (~38:13-38:26).

Case 4 (knee), week 5, is a separate pattern, not an instance of team-rhythm alignment: running frequency was deliberately reduced to two larger-load sessions "in order to make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions," explicitly to bridge into "a larger rehab focus session which was designed as a session that was comparable to match loads in order to prepare for a return to play," planned for week 6 (~37:24-38:11). That week-6 session is a pre-RTP match-load rehearsal, distinct from the team-week-shaping pattern described above.

**Why it works** — For the Case 4 frequency cut, Harries states the reason directly: reducing running frequency let him "make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions" so there was "a nice little progression into" the larger, match-comparable session planned for the following week (~37:26-37:55). For the broader practice of shaping rehab-week structure around the team's rhythm, his only stated reason is the week-7 mid-week session "aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season" (~38:20-38:22); he gives no further explicit rationale for the general practice. Inference (entry writer's): tying rehab-session load to the team's own hard/light day pattern lets the returning athlete's tolerance build in step with what full training will actually demand in the week he returns, rather than on a schedule disconnected from it.

**When to apply** — When designing a returning athlete's week once he is off an isolated running-only schedule and beginning to overlap with team sessions (typically mid-to-late rehab, alongside modified/partial training participation). Eric's review (Review and Plan line 75, "Linear → undulating" row): "You already undulate load across the team week"; the gap it fills is "the same logic applied to one returning player, anchored to the team's Tue/Wed high, Thu low pattern." That remark is about linear-then-undulating MV progression (see [[heuristic--linear-then-undulating-mv-progression]]), not this week-shaping pattern directly. Inference: the same anchor fits the week-shape pattern in this entry.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries never states this as a fixed template; no claim is made that a "high-moderate-high" week or a captain's-run walkthrough is required, and the specific weekly shapes differ across all three cases that show them, tracking each athlete's own timeline and injury type. Case outcomes only (n=3), no outcome data. Do not import a specific case's weekly pattern wholesale as a template; use the underlying idea, build the rehab week around the team's actual week, and rebuild the specific days for each returning athlete.

**Example** — See [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]], weeks 5-7, for the clearest stated rationale: a frequency cut used as a deliberate bridge to a larger session, and an RTP week deliberately matched to the team's normal in-season training rhythm.

# The Mid-Rehab Checkpoint: ~85% MV Around Day 10-14 for Hamstring-Type Injuries

**What it is** — Harries gives a calendar anchor, matched to force-production, reactive-strength and healing-time criteria. Inference: these line up with the general 75-85% MV gate (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]). Inference: his "this type of injury" reads as the hamstring-type strains of Cases 1-2. Describing session 5 (stated as "identical to session five in case one," ~19:47-19:56), he says it "probably represents a typical mid stage max velocity progression for this type of injury at about the 10 [to] 14 day post injury mark" (~19:56-20:04) and, discussing the same session a few lines later, that it "typifies the point in rehab where you push towards around about 85% max velocity at that day 14 type mark, plus or minus, but rarely would you go beyond that. Most would consider this a bit of a sound ceiling until further force production or reactive strength criteria are confirmed, as well as some adequate time for biological healing" (~20:40-21:02). He calls the timing "typical" (19:58); "most would consider" refers to the ~85% ceiling (20:53). He adds that the session structure "could be employed slightly earlier or held slightly later, depending on how the athlete's responding" (~20:08-20:14). The transcript literally reads "10 day 14 post injury mark," almost certainly an ASR-dropped "to"; read as "10 to 14 day."

**Why it works** — Practitioner ceiling. The day-10-14 anchor itself is stated as "typical", with no stated dispute. He frames ~85% as a ceiling to hold until force-production and reactive-strength criteria are confirmed and healing time has passed (20:51-21:00). He gives no physiological mechanism for why day 10-14 specifically is the natural point for this pause; the timing is presented as his stated clinical experience ("most would consider," "typical"), not a derived rule.

**When to apply** — As a rough calendar anchor for planning when a hamstring-type strain rehab should reach the 75-85% MV gate, so force-production and reactive-strength testing (Nordic, isometric benchmarks, hop test; see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]) can be scheduled around day 10-14 rather than left open-ended. Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that Baylor has no documented phased RTP timeline of its own yet; this gives a starting calendar reference to validate against Baylor's own returning-athlete data.

**When NOT to apply** — This is stated for "this type of injury," meaning the hamstring-type strains of Cases 1-2. Harries treats the calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]], discussed later in the same module, ~27:00 onward) as a deliberately different, lower-frequency injury pattern; do not apply the day-10-14 anchor to that case, or to a joint/ligament case such as [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]], which was straight-line-only for sessions 1-6 (braced for the first few runs), with light introductory change-of-direction drills in session 5 (Part 6 41:04-41:27). This is expert opinion ("most would consider"), not a validated cutoff. The 20:40-21:02 passage itself names no specific numbers; it defers to the force-production and reactive-strength criteria set out in [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]], whose specific benchmark figures (1.7-1.8x BW calf, 80-85% pre-injury hamstring) that entry already flags as AFL-context, citation-free numbers. The criteria this checkpoint defers to are disputed by Harries' own account: "there are of course varied opinions in the field on this criteria" (Part 3 15:21-15:26). The day-10-14 timing itself is not disputed in the source.

**Example** — In [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] and [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]], session 5 (identical structure in both) sits at this checkpoint: six 60 m strides, two each at 70-75%, 75-80% and ~82.5% MV.

**Related** — [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] (the general force-production/healing/reactive-strength criteria this checkpoint time-anchors); [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] (the calf case this checkpoint explicitly does not describe); [[research-papers/wollin-2020-a-novel-hamstring-strain-injury-prevention-system-post-match-strength-testing-for-secondar]]. Also summarized in [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] (line 18); this entry is the standalone, findable form, written because the round-1 review asked for the checkpoint to exist as its own entry.

# HSR/VHSR Delivery Shifts in Hamstring-Type Rehab: Structured Repeats, Then Short Intervals, Then Small-Sided Games

**What it is** — In the hamstring-type cases (Case 1, Case 2), high-speed running (HSR/VHSR) volume is delivered through three successive formats as rehab advances. Early sessions accumulate HSR through structured, individually-prescribed repeats over a fixed distance (e.g. 100 m and 60 m repeats). From around mid-rehab (session 5 in Case 1, session 3 in Case 2), HSR shifts to short interval formats: "10 seconds on, 10 seconds off, or 15 seconds on and off" (Case 1, ~10:17-10:35), and "short interval, high intensity interval training formats, like 10 seconds on, 10 seconds off, 20 seconds on, 20 seconds off" (Case 2, ~23:14-23:22). From around session 7-8, small-sided games and technical/tactical drills start to contribute HSR/VHSR "a little bit more meaningfully" or "more organically," alongside whatever prescribed running work continues (Case 1, ~10:35-10:46; Case 2, ~23:25-23:30). Case 4, a knee-joint case run straight-line-only for sessions 1-6 (braced for the first few runs, except very light introductory change-of-direction drills in session 5, 41:04-41:27), reaches the same small-sided-games stage at session 8: "small-sided games, so modified rehab specific drills and also partial participation with the team" (~41:34-41:40). Case 4 supports the small-sided-games stage of the shift, not the earlier two formats. Harries reports a separate, linear VHSR/sprint increase from sessions 4-8 in the same passage (~41:43-41:46) without explicitly linking the two statements.

**Why it works** — Harries does not give an explicit mechanism for why the delivery format itself should shift (his only nearby general statement is that session structure "could be employed slightly earlier or held slightly later, depending on how the athlete's responding," said of the mid-rehab checkpoint, not this format shift specifically, ~20:08-20:14). Inference (entry writer's): moving from individually-prescribed, fixed-distance repeats to short intervals to game-based drills lets the athlete accumulate the same category of high-speed exposure in progressively less predictable, more sport-representative contexts, without needing to represcribe every rep once basic mechanics and pacing are established.

**When to apply** — Inference: a usable default for programming HSR/VHSR volume in hamstring-type rehab, once basic linear mechanics and pacing are established (roughly Level 1-2, see [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]). Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that Baylor has no documented phased RTP protocol of its own, and its GPS thresholds are generic and vendor-organized, not sport-specific. Inference: this three-stage shift could be paired with those thresholds.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries never states this as a fixed session-count rule; the session numbers cited here (5, 3, 7, 8) are case-specific, not a stated formula, and the source's own repeated caveat is that the framework is a guide adjusted to context, not a step-by-step protocol (see [[principle--framework-is-a-guide-not-a-protocol]]). Case 3 (recurrent calf) did not follow this: intervals went short-to-long and HSR was held at 30-40% of match load without progression (Part 6 31:24-32:04). Harries contrasts this with hamstring rehab, which "might more commonly use a long to short approach" (see [[heuristic--short-to-long-vs-long-to-short-intervals-by-injury]]; [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]). The Case 4 example also shows the small-sided-games stage can run alongside other, unrelated restrictions (change-of-direction was withheld, apart from light session-5 drills, through session 6 there for bracing reasons); do not treat "small-sided games by session 7-8" as evidence that all restrictions lift on that same timeline. Do not import a specific case's session numbers as a prescription.

**Example** — In [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]], HSR moved from 100 m repeats (session 2, which overshot the low 17 km/h threshold, see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]) to short intervals (session 3) to small-sided games contributing HSR organically (session 8).

# Fitting Rehab Sessions Into the Team's Own Training Week

**What it is** — In Cases 1, 2 and 4, once the athlete overlaps with team training, the rehab week is shaped around the team's week: Case 2 "started to fall into the team's training structure a bit more" (17:40-17:44), and Case 4's RTP week was "aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season" (38:20-38:22). Case 2, week 3: a small on-field rehab session early in the week, a return to partial training midweek, then "a larger combined rehab session with modified team training" at week's end (~17:45-17:56). Case 2, week 4: two non-consecutive training days then two consecutive days, the second-to-last being "a captain's run walkthrough style session, though very low intensity," followed by return to play in a match (~17:56-18:10). Case 1, week 3: "a high moderate high structure, including partial training exposure in the midweek, and a heavier modified training session on the weekend" (~05:18-05:27). Case 1, week 4: "one light partial session, a full training midweek, and a walkthrough style session... And then they played their game at the end of the week" (~05:27-05:37). Case 4, week 7 (the RTP week): "a small session early in the week, a moderate session mid-week, which was aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season," then return to play at week's end (~38:13-38:26).

Case 4 (knee), week 5, is a separate pattern, not an instance of team-rhythm alignment: running frequency was deliberately reduced to two larger-load sessions "in order to make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions," explicitly to bridge into "a larger rehab focus session which was designed as a session that was comparable to match loads in order to prepare for a return to play," planned for week 6 (~37:24-38:11). That week-6 session is a pre-RTP match-load rehearsal, distinct from the team-week-shaping pattern described above.

**Why it works** — For the Case 4 frequency cut, Harries states the reason directly: reducing running frequency let him "make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions" so there was "a nice little progression into" the larger, match-comparable session planned for the following week (~37:26-37:55). For the broader practice of shaping rehab-week structure around the team's rhythm, his only stated reason is the week-7 mid-week session "aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season" (~38:20-38:22); he gives no further explicit rationale for the general practice. Inference (entry writer's): tying rehab-session load to the team's own hard/light day pattern lets the returning athlete's tolerance build in step with what full training will actually demand in the week he returns, rather than on a schedule disconnected from it.

**When to apply** — When designing a returning athlete's week once he is off an isolated running-only schedule and beginning to overlap with team sessions (typically mid-to-late rehab, alongside modified/partial training participation). Eric's review (Review and Plan line 75, "Linear → undulating" row): "You already undulate load across the team week"; the gap it fills is "the same logic applied to one returning player, anchored to the team's Tue/Wed high, Thu low pattern." That remark is about linear-then-undulating MV progression (see [[heuristic--linear-then-undulating-mv-progression]]), not this week-shaping pattern directly. Inference: the same anchor fits the week-shape pattern in this entry.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries never states this as a fixed template; no claim is made that a "high-moderate-high" week or a captain's-run walkthrough is required, and the specific weekly shapes differ across all three cases that show them, tracking each athlete's own timeline and injury type. Case outcomes only (n=3), no outcome data. Do not import a specific case's weekly pattern wholesale as a template; use the underlying idea, build the rehab week around the team's actual week, and rebuild the specific days for each returning athlete.

**Example** — See [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]], weeks 5-7, for the clearest stated rationale: a frequency cut used as a deliberate bridge to a larger session, and an RTP week deliberately matched to the team's normal in-season training rhythm.
